title: 13 Ways To Avoid Being A Stressed-Out Teacher
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that reducing teaching-related stress requires concrete action, not just wishing for a better year, and offers 13 specific strategies to deploy before the pressure of a new school year sets in. The list spans following the classroom management plan (the single most important item), saying no to distractions, cutting inefficiency, limiting talking, deciding each morning to stay calm, breathing and visualizing, refusing to react in anger, treating consequence-enforcement like refereeing, deliberately limiting prep time to force focus, shifting responsibilities onto students, keeping the room tidy, and maintaining outside interests to preserve balance. He closes by directing readers to his own archive and book for deeper coverage of each item, and stresses that the goal isn't accumulating more items to check off a list but converting these strategies into automatic habits that no longer require conscious effort.
points: Following the classroom management plan is named the single most effective stress-reducer, ahead of all 12 other strategies on the list.
Deliberately limiting your own prep time forces heightened focus and often produces better-quality lessons than unlimited prep time would.
Shifting appropriate responsibilities onto students reduces teacher stress while benefiting students' own progress.
Maintaining interests outside of school — hobbies, faith, family — that matter more than teaching keeps work life in balance and reduces stress.
The goal isn't accumulating more items to consciously check off each day, but converting the 13 strategies into automatic habits over time.
quotes: You can’t just talk about your teaching-related stress. You have to do something about it. You have to make changes.
This is by far the most important. Nothing comes close to alleviating stress more effectively than allowing your classroom management plan to do its job curbing misbehavior.
By limiting the time you allow to prepare for class, and thus forcing a heightened level of focus, you’ll amaze yourself not only what you accomplish but how much better the quality is.

Most teachers take on, at least to some degree, what should be their students’ responsibilities. The more you hand over to them, however, the better for them and their progress and less stress for you.
Having interests outside of school that are more important to you than teaching—like certain hobbies, faith, or family—keeps your work life in balance, thereby reducing stress.
The idea, however, isn’t to have more things to check off your daily list. It’s to turn your new skills into habits you no longer have to think about.
